prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the very near walls/pillars from the recessed brick area, person, pan, railings, and distant construction scene; approximate scale from the RGB suggests the walls are within about 0.2–0.6 m, the bricks about 1–2 m away, and the outdoor background several metres away. Across frames 2–5, the person remains roughly 0.7–1.5 m in front of the camera wearer while shifting from centre-left to centre and then right; the pan stays about 0.7–1.2 m away and generally left of the person, with the person and pan within roughly an arm's length of each other. The map makes foreground occlusion especially clear: a near pillar blocks much of frame 2, and nearby wall edges partly hide the recessed space and outdoor background as the viewpoint turns. Brightness is not a calibrated metric and is inconsistent on the person, pan, thin railings, and distant surfaces, so exact distances and whether the person approaches slightly or merely changes image position are unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies a small carrot-like object in the recessed left area of frame 1 and a person in frames 2–5, isolating their silhouettes even where clothing, shadows, and the construction background reduce RGB contrast. The person moves from centre-left to centre and then to the right side of view, remaining approximately 0.7–1.5 m in front of the camera wearer; the carrot is roughly 1–2 m away, left of the later person positions, while the nearby pan, walls, bricks, poles, and railings are not labelled. The masks clarify which visible regions belong to the person and show partial self-occlusion around the arms and legs, but they provide no direct metric depth, facing direction, or reliable arm's-reach measurement without the RGB and depth context. The duplicated person labels in frame 3, coarse body boundaries, missing carrot after frame 1, and failure to segment the pan and scene structure make object counts, small separations, and occluded parts unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map places the person's torso and limbs in frames 2, 3, and 5, showing them about 0.7–1.5 m ahead and changing from a left-leaning posture near centre-left to a more upright position near centre and then near the right edge. Their shoulders and torso are mostly oriented toward the camera wearer, with the head generally facing forward or slightly downward, but the sparse facial points cannot establish gaze reliably. The limb geometry shows the hands below the torso and near the person's own reachable space, while the camera wearer’s reach, the pan, carrot, walls, and other scene objects are not represented; in frame 5, lower-body parts approach the image boundary and some limbs overlap in projection. Pose is completely missing in frames 1 and 4 despite the person being visible in frame 4, and several face, hand, and leg keypoints appear noisy or anatomically displaced, so precise joint locations, occlusions, and approach or retreat are unreliable.
